Adult Peacock cichlids (Cichla orinocensis) attain a maximum total length of 61.7 cm [Li = 61.7 cm], a size that positions them as one of the larger members of their genus within South American river systems. Females reach reproductive maturity at a considerably smaller size, with total length at puberty recorded at 28 cm [Lp = 28 cm], reflecting a pronounced sexual dimorphism in body dimensions that is common among piscivorous cichlids. The wet weight at puberty for females is approximately 323 g [Wwp = approximately 323 g], estimated from length-weight regressions derived from field-collected specimens. This body mass at maturation stands in stark contrast to the ultimate wet weight, which can reach 3568 g [Wwi = 3568 g] in large, dominant individuals. Such a substantial increase in mass from puberty to adulthood suggests a prolonged period of somatic investment after sexual maturation, likely tied to the energetic demands of defending territories and securing high-quality foraging grounds in the flooded forest and riverine habitats they occupy.

Under controlled laboratory conditions at a stable water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the age at birth for newly emerged yolk-sac larvae is approximately 8.1 days [ab = approximately 8.1 days], encompassing both embryonic development and the subsequent yolk sac absorption phase. This relatively rapid transition from fertilized egg to free-swimming larva is characteristic of many Neotropical cichlids, though it is notably shorter than in some substrate-brooding congeners. During this early life stage, the larvae are entirely dependent on endogenous yolk reserves, and the timing of first exogenous feeding is tightly coupled to the completion of yolk sac resorption. The wet weight at birth is estimated at 0.0042 g [Wwb = 0.0042 g], a value derived from egg diameter measurements of related cichlid species and reflecting the small initial size of the offspring at the moment of chorion rupture.

At a water temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C], the maximum daily reproduction rate for Peacock cichlids has been characterized through both field observations and captive breeding studies, yielding an annualized output of approximately 274 eggs per year [Ri = approximately 274 eggs per year]. This annual reproductive strategy is consistent with the species' role as a capital breeder in highly seasonal floodplain environments, where spawning is synchronized with the rising water levels that provide abundant nursery habitat for the offspring. Under these thermal conditions, females produce approximately 274 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 274 eggs per clutch], and they can complete up to a single spawning event each year [F_R_i = single spawning event each year], though both sub-expressions together yield the maximum annual fecundity noted. The relatively modest clutch size, when compared to other large-bodied cichlids, suggests a trade-off between egg number and the intensive parental care that both parents provide, guarding the brood and fanning the eggs to ensure adequate oxygenation throughout the incubation period.

Longevity data for Cichla orinocensis indicate a maximum lifespan of approximately 8 years [am = approximately 8 years] when measured under captive conditions at 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This lifespan is typical for a large, slow-growing cichlid that invests heavily in somatic growth and territorial defense, and it aligns with the life-history expectations for a predatory fish occupying a relatively stable, though seasonally variable, tropical environment. Field studies suggest that individuals in natural populations may experience somewhat shorter lifespans due to predation and fishing pressure, but the fundamental physiological senescence pattern remains evident. The sustained growth observed throughout much of the adult life, culminating in the large asymptotic sizes described earlier, is a hallmark of indeterminate growth, and it allows older females to produce increasingly larger clutches as they accumulate body mass. 

The extreme vulnerability of the larval stage at a birth mass of 0.0042 g [Wwb = 0.0042 g] at 25 °C [T = 25 °C] is offset by dense aquatic vegetation, which provides shelter from predators in the flooded forest and riverine habitats typical of the Orinoco basin. Habitats that offer complex submerged structure are therefore critical for early survival, and the availability of such microhabitats can strongly influence year-class strength. In comparison to the ultimate wet weight of 3568 g [Wwi = 3568 g], the neonate's mass represents an increase of over five orders of magnitude across the species' life span of 8 years [am = 8 years], a growth trajectory that demands consistently high food intake and efficient assimilation at a temperature of 25 °C [T = 25 °C]. This energetic pathway constrains the maximum reproduction rate and reinforces the role of biparental care as a cornerstone of the species' demographic strategy.
